VA-11 Hall-A: Cyberpunk Bartender Action

Sukeban Games’s bartending visual novel: pixel-art characters in a neon-lit bar in Glitch City, framed by a screen of dark, outlined interface panels.

Source
Steam: VA-11 Hall-A: Cyberpunk Bartender Action
Creator
Sukeban Games
Made
2016 (released 21 June 2016 for Windows, macOS, and Linux)
Styles
Cyberpunk (agent-proposed, not yet reviewed by a person), Pixel Art (agent-proposed, not yet reviewed by a person)

Evidence
Downloaded and inspected eight 1920 × 1080 px screenshots from the Steam store listing (app 447530) in a scratch folder. The observations come from the two bar screenshots with the drink-mixing panel.
Reviewed
2 October 2026
Rights
Link and metadata only. License: unverified. Rights policy

Context

Wikipedia: “VA-11 Hall-A: Cyberpunk Bartender Action … is a 2016 visual novel developed by Venezuelan studio Sukeban Games and published by Ysbryd Games.” It was first released for Windows, OS X, and Linux on 21 June 2016. Wikipedia.

Wikipedia: “The game features a retro-futuristic look based on cyberpunk media, PC-98 games, and anime-inspired visuals.” Corruption and food shortages “run rampant” in Glitch City, where the bar is. Wikipedia.

Observed

  • The screen is a frame of near-black and dark violet panels with thin outlines and small notches along the top edge.
  • The left panel shows the bar in pixel art: magenta and violet walls, a blue neon logo reading “KIRIRIN Light”, a pink neon bottle, and two round cyan-and-red gauges.
  • At top right, “Cyberpunk Bartender Action” in thin pink type sits above “VA-11 HALL-A” in heavy italic pink capitals.
  • The mixing panel is a grid of outlined cells labelled “Adelhyde”, “Bronson Ext”, “Pwd Delta”, “Flanergide”, and “Karmotrine” in a monospace pixel font, with gray beveled buttons “Reset”, “Mix”, “Slot 1”, and “Slot 2”.
  • Dialogue appears in a black box at the bottom, with the speaker’s name in magenta or blue (“Dorothy:”, “Jill:”) and the text in white monospace.

Why it belongs

The game reduces the style to a few interface rules (dark panels, outlined cells, monospace labels, neon accents) and shows that they work at a low resolution.

Its beveled gray buttons and anime characters pull it toward pixel art and away from the strict HUD look.

Borrow

Color the speaker’s name, not the message, when you put dialogue or log lines in neon on black.

Lay out controls as a grid of outlined cells, each with a short monospace label.
